stem: A security engineer wants a fully managed threat detection service that continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs, and CloudTrail management events to identify malicious or unauthorized behavior, without deploying any agents or sensors. Which AWS service BEST fits this requirement?
options: Amazon GuardDuty, which continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events using threat intelligence and machine learning to generate findings with no agents required.
AWS Config, which records resource configuration changes and evaluates them against rules.
Amazon Inspector, which scans EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities.
AWS Trusted Advisor, which reviews the account against best-practice checks across cost, performance, and security.
explanation: Amazon GuardDuty is an agentless threat detection service that continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs, and CloudTrail management events (plus S3 and EKS data events when those protection plans are enabled) against threat intelligence feeds and machine learning models to produce findings, with nothing to deploy or manage. AWS Config tracks configuration compliance, not threat behavior. Amazon Inspector finds software vulnerabilities in workloads, not behavioral threats in account activity. Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations across several categories but does not perform continuous behavioral threat detection.

stem: A company runs AWS Organizations with 40 member accounts and wants GuardDuty enabled in every account and every Region automatically as new accounts are created, with findings visible from one central account, without each account owner having to enable GuardDuty manually. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Enable GuardDuty independently in each of the 40 accounts and export findings to a shared Amazon S3 bucket using a scheduled job.

Designate a delegated administrator account for GuardDuty through AWS Organizations, and turn on auto-enable so GuardDuty activates automatically in existing and new member accounts with findings aggregated to the delegated administrator.
Create an AWS Config aggregator in the management account to collect GuardDuty findings from every member account.
Attach a service control policy that requires each account owner to enable GuardDuty within 24 hours of account creation.
explanation: GuardDuty integrates with AWS Organizations: a delegated administrator account can manage GuardDuty for the whole organization, and turning on auto-enable activates GuardDuty automatically for existing and future member accounts, with all findings visible centrally to the delegated administrator, none of which requires per-account manual setup. Enabling it account by account and exporting to S3 on a schedule is exactly the manual, non-automatic approach the requirement rules out. A Config aggregator collects AWS Config compliance data, not GuardDuty findings. An SCP can restrict or require API call patterns, but it cannot itself enable a regional detector or guarantee GuardDuty actually gets turned on, so it does not satisfy 'automatically enabled.'

stem: GuardDuty raises a finding that an EC2 instance's credentials were used from an unusual geographic location. A security analyst wants to quickly understand the full scope of the incident: what this instance's role has done historically, whether the same credentials were used elsewhere, and how this activity connects to other resources and API calls over the past weeks, presented as a visual timeline, without writing custom Athena queries. Which service BEST supports this investigation?
options: Amazon Macie, to classify sensitive data that the instance may have accessed.
AWS Config, to review the instance's configuration history.

Amazon Detective, which automatically builds a behavior graph from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings so an analyst can visually explore related activity and history without writing queries.
AWS Systems Manager Inventory, to list software installed on the instance.
explanation: Amazon Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings, and automatically builds a linked behavior graph so analysts can pivot visually across principals, resources, IP addresses, and time to scope an incident, which is exactly the deep, historical, no-query investigation described. GuardDuty is what raised the finding but is not the visual investigation tool. Macie classifies sensitive data and does not build activity timelines. AWS Config tracks configuration state over time, not API and network behavior. Systems Manager Inventory lists installed software and metadata, not security-relevant historical activity across resources.

stem: A company operates 15 AWS accounts across two Regions and wants a single, unified view of security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and IAM Access Analyzer, normalized into one common finding format, aggregated into one Region for a central security team to triage. Which AWS service BEST meets this requirement?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights, to run ad hoc queries across each account's log groups.
AWS Config aggregator, to collect resource configuration compliance from every account.
AWS Organizations consolidated billing, to view cost data across accounts.

AWS Security Hub, which ingests findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, and partner tools, normalizes them into the AWS Security Finding Format, and can aggregate findings from multiple Regions into one Region.
explanation: AWS Security Hub is purpose-built to collect findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, Config, and partner security products, normalize them into the AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF), and, with finding aggregation enabled, roll up findings from linked Regions into one aggregation Region for centralized triage. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data but does not normalize or aggregate security findings across services. A Config aggregator only covers AWS Config resource compliance, not the broader finding set. Consolidated billing addresses cost visibility, not security findings.

stem: A company enables GuardDuty S3 Protection and later receives a finding indicating that an IAM principal is exhibiting a pattern of unusual API calls that retrieve large numbers of objects from a sensitive S3 bucket, at a volume inconsistent with that principal's history. Which GuardDuty data source made this specific detection possible?
options: S3 Protection, which analyzes S3 data event activity from CloudTrail to detect suspicious access patterns such as unusual API call volume or data exfiltration behavior against a bucket.
VPC Flow Log analysis, which only inspects network traffic metadata at the ENI level and has no visibility into S3 API activity.
Malware Protection for EC2, which scans attached EBS volumes for malicious files.
AWS Config configuration snapshots, which record the bucket's settings but not API call activity.
explanation: GuardDuty S3 Protection consumes S3 data event activity (object-level API calls) from CloudTrail and applies threat intelligence and anomaly detection to flag patterns like unusual data access volume, suspicious API sequences, or requests from anomalous locations, which is exactly the scenario described. VPC Flow Log analysis sees network metadata, not S3 object API semantics, so it could not identify this pattern by itself. Malware Protection for EC2 scans EBS volumes for malware, unrelated to S3 API behavior. AWS Config records configuration state changes, not the API call volume needed to detect this kind of exfiltration pattern.

stem: A team wants automated, continuous scanning of their EC2 instances, container images stored in Amazon ECR, and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and network reachability issues, with a risk score to help prioritize remediation. Which AWS service BEST fits?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor, which offers point-in-time best-practice checks across several categories.

Amazon Inspector, which continuously scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions for known vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, producing a risk score for prioritization.
AWS Config, which evaluates whether resource configurations comply with defined rules.
Amazon GuardDuty, which detects malicious behavior and anomalies from log and network data sources.
explanation: Amazon Inspector continuously and automatically scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities and, for EC2, network reachability issues, and assigns a risk score that blends CVE severity with exploitability and network exposure to help prioritize fixes. Trusted Advisor's security checks are broader but point-in-time best-practice checks, not continuous CVE and reachability scanning. AWS Config evaluates configuration state against rules, not vulnerabilities in installed software. GuardDuty detects behavioral and network threats from logs, not software vulnerabilities in workloads.

stem: A security team wants to detect anomalous account and network behavior using AWS-native machine learning and statistical baselining, without writing and maintaining custom detection rules or thresholds. Which TWO AWS capabilities provide this out of the box? (Select TWO.)
options: AWS Config, which evaluates resources against user-authored or managed rules on a schedule.
Amazon GuardDuty, which applies machine learning and threat intelligence to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs to flag anomalous behavior without any custom rule authoring.
Amazon S3 Storage Lens, which reports storage usage and activity metrics for cost and usage optimization.
AWS CloudTrail Insights, which uses statistical baselining on management event volume to automatically surface unusual API call rates and patterns without configuring thresholds.
AWS Systems Manager Inventory, which catalogs installed software and metadata across managed instances.
explanation: GuardDuty applies machine learning and curated threat intelligence directly to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs to flag anomalies with zero custom rule authoring, and CloudTrail Insights builds a statistical baseline of normal API call volume and automatically surfaces unusual spikes or patterns in management events, again with no thresholds to configure. AWS Config only evaluates against rules a person defines or selects, which is the opposite of automatic anomaly baselining. S3 Storage Lens reports usage metrics for cost and storage optimization, not security anomalies. Systems Manager Inventory catalogs installed software and instance metadata; it does not detect anomalous behavior.

stem: A company runs Amazon EKS clusters and Amazon RDS databases and wants GuardDuty findings that cover suspicious Kubernetes audit log activity, such as privilege escalation attempts within a cluster, as well as anomalous database login behavior, such as a pattern associated with brute-force or credential-stuffing activity against RDS. Which GuardDuty protection plans together cover both scenarios?
options: Malware Protection for EC2 and S3 Protection.
S3 Protection and Lambda Protection.

EKS Protection, which monitors Kubernetes audit logs (and, with Runtime Monitoring, in-cluster behavior) for suspicious activity, together with RDS Protection, which analyzes login activity for anomalous or suspicious database access attempts.
Malware Protection for EC2 and RDS Protection only, since EKS activity is covered by VPC Flow Log analysis alone.
explanation: EKS Protection analyzes Kubernetes audit logs for suspicious cluster activity such as privilege escalation, and its Runtime Monitoring component adds in-cluster behavioral detection, while RDS Protection profiles login activity to flag anomalous or suspicious database login attempts, together covering both scenarios in the question. Malware Protection for EC2 scans EBS volumes for malware and does not see Kubernetes audit events or RDS logins, so pairing it with S3 Protection or with RDS Protection alone still misses the EKS audit-log detection. Lambda Protection detects malicious behavior in Lambda function network activity, unrelated to Kubernetes clusters. VPC Flow Log analysis alone sees network metadata and does not parse Kubernetes audit log semantics, so EKS Protection is still required.

stem: A security analyst confirms that an EC2 instance is compromised and is actively communicating with a known command-and-control server. The team wants to stop the instance from making further outbound connections and prevent lateral movement, while preserving its running state, memory, and attached volumes for later forensic analysis. Which containment action is BEST?
options: Terminate the instance immediately to stop the malicious activity.
Reboot the instance to clear the malicious process from memory.
Detach the instance's IAM instance profile only, leaving its security group and network access unchanged.

Isolate the instance by replacing its security group with one that denies all inbound and outbound traffic (or allows only traffic to a forensic tooling host), keeping the instance running so its memory and volumes remain intact for investigation.
explanation: Replacing the compromised instance's security group with a quarantine group that denies all inbound and outbound traffic (or permits only a narrow forensic path) immediately stops further command-and-control communication and lateral movement while leaving the instance running, which preserves volatile memory state and the attached EBS volumes for forensic imaging. Terminating the instance destroys memory contents and can trigger deletion of volumes, losing evidence. Rebooting clears running processes and in-memory artifacts that a responder needs to analyze. Detaching only the instance profile stops further AWS API abuse from that instance's role but does nothing to stop network-based command-and-control communication or lateral movement over the network, so it is an incomplete containment step by itself.

stem: During an incident, a security team must preserve forensic evidence from a compromised EC2 instance's attached EBS volume without shutting down or otherwise disturbing the running instance, so the evidence can be analyzed later in an isolated forensic account. Which action BEST achieves this while maintaining a defensible chain of custody?
options: Create an EBS snapshot of the volume while the instance continues running, then copy the snapshot to a dedicated, access-restricted forensic account for analysis.
Attach an Amazon S3 bucket policy to the compromised instance's root volume to prevent further writes.
Stop the instance so its EBS volumes are no longer changing, then analyze the volume in place within the production account.
Enable EBS encryption on the volume after the incident to protect the evidence going forward.
explanation: Taking an EBS snapshot captures a point-in-time copy of the volume without stopping the instance, and copying that snapshot into a separate, tightly access-controlled forensic account isolates the evidence from the potentially compromised production environment and establishes a clear, auditable chain of custody for later analysis. An S3 bucket policy has no effect on an EBS volume, since the two are different storage services. Stopping the instance loses volatile memory contents that are often critical to the investigation, and analyzing evidence in place in the production account risks further tampering and weakens chain of custody. Enabling encryption after the fact does not preserve or transfer the evidence and does not address the immediate forensic requirement.

stem: A security team discovers that an IAM user's long-term access key was committed to a public GitHub repository. Which sequence of actions is the BEST immediate response?
options: Wait for GuardDuty to raise a finding before taking any action, since manual intervention could interfere with automated detection.

Immediately deactivate or delete the exposed access key to cut off further use, then review CloudTrail event history for that key to identify any unauthorized actions already taken, and rotate any credentials or secrets the compromised principal could have accessed.
Delete the IAM user entirely without reviewing any activity, since the user can simply be re-created later.
Change the account's root user password, since the root user is the primary concern in an access-key exposure.
explanation: The immediate priority is to cut off further use of the exposed key by deactivating or deleting it, then use CloudTrail event history to determine exactly what the key was used for during the exposure window, followed by rotating any downstream credentials or secrets the compromised principal could reach, since the blast radius may extend beyond the key itself. Waiting for GuardDuty is passive and leaves the key usable in the meantime, and GuardDuty may not even generate a finding depending on how the key is used. Deleting the user without any investigation forfeits the chance to learn what already happened and to scope the damage. The account root user password is unrelated to an IAM user's own access key, and rotating it does nothing to contain this specific exposure.

stem: A security team wants a fully automated response so that whenever GuardDuty generates a high-severity finding indicating a compromised EC2 instance, a quarantine security group is applied to that instance within seconds, with no analyst having to manually trigger the remediation. Which architecture BEST achieves this?
options: Configure a scheduled AWS Config rule that evaluates GuardDuty findings once every 24 hours and reports noncompliant instances.
Have analysts poll the GuardDuty console every few minutes and manually apply the quarantine security group when they see a new high-severity finding.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches high-severity GuardDuty findings and targets a Lambda function that automatically applies the quarantine security group to the affected instance.
Enable GuardDuty S3 Protection so that S3 automatically blocks all public access whenever any finding is generated.
explanation: GuardDuty findings are delivered as events to Amazon EventBridge; an EventBridge rule can match on finding severity or type and invoke a Lambda function that automatically reassigns the quarantine security group to the affected instance, achieving near real-time, fully automated containment with no human trigger. A daily Config rule check is both far too slow for a compromised instance and is not how GuardDuty findings are consumed for automated response. Manual console polling is explicitly the un-automated approach the requirement rules out. Enabling S3 Protection only adds an S3-focused GuardDuty data source and does not perform any EC2 remediation action.

stem: A compromised IAM role's temporary credentials, issued via sts:AssumeRole, are still valid for another 45 minutes and the attacker is actively using them. Deleting or modifying the role's trust policy will not invalidate credentials already issued. Which action immediately invalidates all active sessions issued from this role before their natural expiration?
options: Delete the IAM role entirely, since AWS automatically invalidates any credentials issued from a deleted role within seconds.
Rotate the value of the role's trust policy ExternalId, since active sessions revalidate the trust policy on every API call.
Wait for the credentials to expire naturally, since IAM has no way to revoke temporary credentials early.

Attach or update an inline policy on the role that denies all actions for principals whose credentials were issued before the current time, using the aws:TokenIssueTime condition key, which immediately invalidates every active session from that role regardless of when it expires.
explanation: IAM lets you revoke active sessions for a role by attaching a policy that denies access based on the aws:TokenIssueTime condition key, set to the current time; because every API call made with temporary credentials is evaluated against the role's policies at request time, this immediately blocks all sessions issued before that point, regardless of their remaining validity window. Deleting the role does not carry a documented guarantee of instantly invalidating already-issued credentials on every call, and it also removes the role for any legitimate future use, which is disruptive. The ExternalId condition on a trust policy is checked only during the AssumeRole call itself, not on every subsequent action taken with the resulting credentials, so changing it has no effect on sessions already established. Waiting for natural expiration leaves the attacker's active session usable for the full remaining window, which the scenario says is unacceptable.

stem: An IAM user's long-term access key appears in a public code repository. Which TWO actions should the incident responder take FIRST, before any further investigation? (Select TWO.)
options: Immediately deactivate or delete the exposed access key so it can no longer be used to authenticate.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on all buckets in the account to speed up the eventual audit.
Wait until the next scheduled access review to decide whether the key should be rotated.
Permanently disable AWS CloudTrail logging in the affected Region to reduce noise while investigating.
Review CloudTrail event history for every API call made with the exposed key during the exposure window, to scope what the attacker may have accessed or changed.
explanation: The two immediate priorities are to deactivate or delete the exposed key so it stops working right away, and to review CloudTrail event history for that key to scope exactly what was accessed or changed during the exposure window, which together stop the bleeding and tell the responder what to investigate and remediate next. Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration has nothing to do with containment or investigation. Waiting for a scheduled review leaves a known-compromised key active far too long. Disabling CloudTrail logging is actively harmful: it removes the very audit trail the response depends on and can itself look like an attempt to cover tracks.

stem: A security team triages Security Hub findings manually today. They want specific findings, when an analyst selects them in the console, to automatically kick off a predefined SSM Automation runbook that isolates the affected resource, without the analyst needing to switch to a different tool or copy any details by hand. Which Security Hub capability enables this?
options: A Security Hub custom action, which sends the selected findings as an event to Amazon EventBridge, where a rule can target an SSM Automation runbook, directly or via Lambda, to execute the response.
Security Hub finding aggregation, which consolidates findings from multiple Regions into one Region.
Security Hub consolidated control findings, which reduce duplicate findings for the same control across standards.
A Security Hub insight, which is a saved, grouped view of findings by a chosen attribute.
explanation: A Security Hub custom action lets an analyst select one or more findings in the console and send them as an event to Amazon EventBridge; an EventBridge rule matching that custom action event can target an SSM Automation runbook, directly or through a Lambda function, to execute the isolation response, all without leaving the Security Hub console or copying data manually. Finding aggregation only centralizes findings across Regions and does not trigger any response. Consolidated control findings reduce duplicate findings for the same underlying check, a data-hygiene feature unrelated to triggering automation. An insight is a saved, grouped query for reporting and does not execute any action.

stem: A public-facing web application on an Application Load Balancer is receiving a spike of login attempts using stolen credentials (credential stuffing) mixed into otherwise normal-looking traffic, along with common SQL injection probes. The team wants to block both patterns at the edge, in front of the application, using a managed AWS service, without building and maintaining custom signature rules from scratch. Which approach is BEST?
options: Configure Amazon GuardDuty to inspect ALB access logs for suspicious login patterns and block matching source IPs automatically.

Attach an AWS WAF web ACL to the ALB that combines an AWS Managed Rules rule group such as the SQL database rule group with a rate-based rule to throttle and block sources that exceed a request-rate threshold associated with credential stuffing.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced alone, since it fully inspects HTTP request bodies for SQL injection and credential-stuffing patterns.
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer, which inspects Layer 7 payloads for malicious patterns by default.
explanation: An AWS WAF web ACL attached to the ALB can combine an AWS Managed Rules rule group, such as the SQL database rule group with curated signatures for SQL injection, with a rate-based rule that throttles or blocks sources exceeding a request threshold, addressing both the injection probes and the credential-stuffing volume without writing custom signatures. GuardDuty analyzes logs and network or API behavior for threat findings; it is not an inline Layer 7 blocking control for ALB requests. Shield Advanced protects against DDoS and integrates with WAF, but it does not itself inspect HTTP payloads for SQL injection or credential-stuffing patterns; that inspection is WAF's job. A Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and has no visibility into HTTP request content, so switching to NLB adds no Layer 7 protection.

stem: An internet-facing application on Amazon EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer is a frequent target of large-scale network and transport layer DDoS attacks. The company wants proactive DDoS cost protection, access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) during active attacks, and health-based, near-real-time detection of degraded application health tied to a Route 53 health check. Which AWS capability BEST meets all of these needs?
options: AWS WAF rate-based rules alone, since they mitigate all layers of DDoS attacks including network-layer floods.
The AWS Shield standard tier, which is automatically included for every AWS customer at no additional cost.

AWS Shield Advanced, which adds DDoS cost protection, 24/7 access to the DRT, and health-based detection that uses a Route 53 or Route 53 Application Recovery Controller health check to improve detection accuracy for a protected resource.
Amazon CloudFront alone, since simply placing a CDN in front of an origin eliminates the need for any DDoS-specific protection.
explanation: AWS Shield Advanced is the paid tier that adds DDoS cost protection for scaling charges incurred during an attack, 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team, and health-based detection, which correlates a resource's health, via an associated Route 53 or Route 53 Application Recovery Controller health check, with traffic anomalies to improve detection accuracy and speed. WAF rate-based rules operate at Layer 7 and help with HTTP floods, but they do not provide DRT access, cost protection, or health-based detection, and they do not mitigate network-layer floods by themselves. Shield Standard is included automatically for all customers but does not include DRT access, cost protection, or health-based detection; those are Advanced-only capabilities. CloudFront helps absorb and distribute traffic but does not by itself provide the cost protection, DRT engagement, or health-based detection features described.

stem: A security engineer configures a network ACL on a subnet to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, but forgets to add an outbound rule allowing the corresponding ephemeral return-traffic ports. Meanwhile, the subnet's EC2 instances have a security group that allows inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no explicit outbound rules configured. What is the MOST likely outcome for HTTPS responses from the instances back to clients?
options: Responses fail, because security groups are stateless and require an explicit outbound rule to allow the return traffic.
Responses succeed, because network ACLs are stateful and automatically allow return traffic regardless of outbound rules.
Responses fail only if the instance is in a public subnet, and succeed in a private subnet.

Responses fail, because network ACLs are stateless and the missing outbound rule for ephemeral ports blocks the return traffic, even though the security group is stateful and would otherwise auto-allow the response given its default outbound-allow-all rule.
explanation: Network ACLs are stateless: an allowed inbound request does not automatically permit its response, so the subnet's NACL needs an explicit outbound rule permitting the ephemeral port range, typically 1024-65535, back to the client, and without it the response is dropped at the NACL. In contrast, security groups are stateful, meaning a security group evaluates only the inbound rule for the request and then automatically allows the matching response, so the security group here, which allows inbound 443 and by default allows all outbound, is not the blocker. Claiming security groups need an explicit outbound rule for return traffic gets statefulness backwards. Claiming NACLs are stateful and auto-allow return traffic is also backwards. Subnet type, public or private, does not change NACL statelessness, so the outcome does not depend on that distinction here.

stem: A company must allow outbound traffic from a VPC only to a specific allow-list of corporate SaaS domains, for example *.salesforce.com, and deny all other outbound internet destinations, including cases where the destination's underlying IP address rotates. Security groups and network ACLs filter only by IP address and port, not by domain name. Which AWS service BEST enforces this domain-based egress control?
options: AWS Network Firewall, using a stateful rule group with domain list rules (an allow list) that matches on domain name, including via TLS SNI for HTTPS, regardless of the destination IP address.
Security groups with an outbound rule referencing a prefix list for each SaaS provider's published IP ranges.
Network ACLs with a deny-all outbound rule and no allow entries.
AWS WAF, attached to the VPC's internet gateway, using a geographic match rule.
explanation: AWS Network Firewall stateful rule groups support domain list rules that match traffic against domain names, including HTTPS traffic via the TLS SNI field, so an allow list can key off the domain itself rather than needing to track the provider's underlying IP addresses, which is exactly what a rotating-IP SaaS destination requires. Security groups and network ACLs filter only on IP address, port, and protocol, so a prefix list still depends on the provider publishing, and you maintaining, accurate IP ranges, which does not solve rotating or unpublished IPs cleanly. A NACL with no allow entries simply blocks everything and provides no way to allow specific domains. WAF is a Layer 7 HTTP(S) inspection service for inbound web traffic to resources like an ALB or CloudFront, and it is not attached to a VPC internet gateway to filter general outbound VPC traffic; a geographic match rule also filters by request origin country, not by destination domain.

stem: A company runs EC2 instances in a private subnet with no internet gateway or NAT gateway, and the instances must read and write objects in Amazon S3 without any traffic ever traversing the public internet. Which solution BEST meets this requirement at the lowest cost?
options: Add a NAT gateway to the private subnet so instances can reach the S3 public endpoint over the internet.
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 and add a route to it in the subnet's route table, which lets instances reach S3 privately over the AWS network with no hourly endpoint charge.
Attach a public IP address to each instance so it can reach S3 directly.
Configure AWS Direct Connect to a corporate data center and route S3 traffic through it.
explanation: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 (or DynamoDB) adds a route in the subnet's route table that sends S3-bound traffic over AWS's private network instead of the internet, and gateway endpoints have no hourly charge, making this the lowest-cost, fully private option. A NAT gateway would route traffic out toward the internet path to the S3 public endpoint and also incurs hourly and data processing charges, so it neither meets the 'no internet' requirement nor is it the lowest cost. Attaching public IP addresses directly contradicts the private-subnet, no-internet-traversal requirement. Direct Connect links to an on-premises data center and is unrelated to reaching an AWS service privately from within the same VPC, and it is far more expensive than a gateway endpoint for this purpose.

stem: A security team wants to eliminate SSH bastion hosts, open inbound SSH security group rules, and long-lived SSH key management for administrative access to EC2 instances, while retaining full audit logs of every interactive session and the ability to enforce IAM-based access control. Which AWS capability BEST replaces bastion-based SSH access?
options: A hardened bastion host with key rotation automated by AWS Secrets Manager.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, so administrators connect over an encrypted tunnel before using SSH as before.

AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, which provides browser-based or CLI shell access to managed instances through the SSM Agent without opening any inbound ports, using IAM policies for authorization and optionally logging session activity to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
A third-party jump box running in a public subnet with multi-factor authentication for SSH logins.
explanation: Systems Manager Session Manager lets administrators start an interactive shell to a managed instance through the SSM Agent's outbound connection to the Systems Manager service, so no inbound port, including SSH, ever needs to be opened, access is governed entirely by IAM policy, and session activity can be logged for audit to CloudWatch Logs or S3, which removes the bastion host, the open SSH rule, and the SSH key management all at once. A hardened bastion with rotated keys still requires an open SSH path and key management, just automated. A Site-to-Site VPN still requires an SSH port and key-based (or similarly managed) authentication once connected. A public jump box, even with MFA on SSH, still exposes an SSH listener and requires SSH key or password management, which is exactly what the team wants to remove.

stem: A company's AWS Organization has 60 accounts. Individual account teams have been inconsistently applying AWS WAF rules and security group baselines, leaving several accounts exposed. Central security wants to mandate a common WAF web ACL and a baseline security group across all current and future accounts and Regions in the organization, enforced centrally rather than relying on each account team to opt in. Which AWS service BEST achieves this centralized, organization-wide enforcement?
options: AWS Config conformance packs, which can evaluate compliance but cannot themselves create or attach a WAF web ACL or a security group to resources.
IAM permission boundaries applied to each account's administrators, restricting which WAF actions they may call.
A service control policy that denies the ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress action across the organization.

AWS Firewall Manager, which centrally creates and enforces a common WAF policy and a common security group policy across all accounts and Regions in an AWS Organization, automatically applying them to new accounts and in-scope resources as they appear.
explanation: AWS Firewall Manager lets a Firewall Manager administrator define a common WAF policy and a common security group policy once, then automatically applies and continuously enforces them across all existing and new accounts and Regions in an AWS Organization, which is exactly the centralized, no-opt-in enforcement the requirement describes. Config conformance packs can evaluate compliance and even trigger remediation via SSM Automation documents, but a conformance pack itself does not create or attach a WAF web ACL or a security group the way a Firewall Manager policy does. IAM permission boundaries constrain what actions administrators can call, but they do not create or enforce any WAF or security group configuration. An SCP blocking a specific security group action can prevent certain changes but does not create the mandated WAF web ACL or a baseline security group, and it does not adapt automatically as new accounts join.

stem: A company must apply operating system security patches to hundreds of EC2 instances across multiple accounts on a recurring monthly schedule, automatically scan for missing patches, and report compliance without manually connecting to each instance. Which AWS Systems Manager capability BEST fits this requirement?
options: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, which uses patch baselines to define approved patches, scans managed instances for missing patches, and can install them on a recurring schedule via a maintenance window, with compliance reporting.
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, which stores configuration values and secrets for retrieval by applications.
AWS Systems Manager Inventory, which only collects metadata about installed software and does not install patches.
Amazon Inspector, which detects vulnerabilities but does not install or schedule patch deployment.
explanation: Patch Manager uses patch baselines to define which patches are approved for each instance's operating system, automatically scans managed instances, registered via the SSM Agent, for missing patches, can install them on a recurring cadence through a maintenance window, and reports patch compliance centrally, matching every part of the requirement. Parameter Store is a configuration and secrets store, unrelated to patching. Inventory catalogs installed software and instance metadata but does not scan for missing patches or install anything. Amazon Inspector identifies vulnerabilities and assigns risk scores but does not itself install patches or run a patch maintenance schedule.

stem: A team is designing subnet-level and instance-level network controls for a VPC and needs to correctly describe how security groups differ from network ACLs. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A network ACL evaluates rules by applying the first matching rule regardless of its rule number, and ignores any lower-numbered rule that also matches.
A security group can contain explicit deny rules to block specific IP addresses.
A network ACL is stateless, so it evaluates inbound and outbound traffic independently and requires explicit rules in both directions, including for return traffic.
A security group operates at the subnet level and automatically applies to every instance launched into that subnet.
A security group is stateful, so a response to an allowed inbound request is automatically permitted outbound regardless of any outbound rule, and vice versa for an outbound-initiated request.
explanation: Network ACLs are stateless, so inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated independently against explicit numbered rules, and a NACL needs its own outbound rule to permit the response to any inbound request it allows, unlike a firewall that tracks connection state. Security groups are stateful: once a security group's rule allows a request in one direction, the corresponding response in the other direction is automatically allowed regardless of any rule for that direction. A network ACL evaluates rules in numeric order and stops at the first match, so a matching rule with a lower number does take precedence over a later, higher-numbered rule, which makes the 'ignores rule number' framing backwards. Security groups support only allow rules, never explicit deny rules; to block traffic you simply omit an allow rule. Security groups are attached directly to elastic network interfaces, and therefore to specific instances, not automatically to every instance in a subnet; that subnet-wide automatic association describes a network ACL, not a security group.
